function.description: A comprehensive document-processing agent capable of extracting, analyzing, and structuring content from a wide range of local office files and text formats. Supports CSV/TSV, Word (DOC/DOCX), PowerPoint (PPT/PPTX), Excel (XLS/XLSX), PDF, and diverse text/code files. Provides unified text extraction, table and media extraction, metadata collection, structural analysis, and multi-format output (Markdown/JSON/HTML/Text). Designed to deliver clean, organized results for downstream reasoning and further processing. It can extract embedded media as raw files or generate screenshots for visual spreadsheet elements, which are then passed to specialized agents for further analysis.

function.name: MediaAnalyzer
function.description: A multimedia analysis agent capable of handling local images, audio, and video. It provides OCR extraction, AI-based visual understanding, metadata inspection, audio transcription and trimming, video analysis and summarization, and key-frame extraction. Supports common formats across images (JPG/PNG/GIF/TIFF/WEBP …), audio (MP3/WAV/FLAC/AAC/OGG …), and video (MP4/AVI/MOV/MKV/WEBM …). GIF and video content are processed as multi-frame sequences—similar to video key-frame extraction—while static image formats are analyzed as single frames. Designed to perform assigned multimedia tasks efficiently and return clear, structured results.

function.name: PythonExecutor
function.description: An agent that can execute Python code snippets in an isolated container environment, similar to running cells in a Jupyter Notebook. Its execution is strictly limited to the Python code and data explicitly provided to it. Useful for performing math calculations or demonstrating small code examples.

function.name: Reasoner
function.description: A reasoning specialist agent equipped with a high-capacity reasoning model. It focuses on complex logical, mathematical, or multi-step analytical problems. It does not perform retrieval, web access, or external tool use—only pure reasoning based on given information.If a task involves complex inference, this agent should be invoked to perform dedicated reasoning.Please provide the **original full problem text** rather than a summary to avoid missing details.

function.name: TerminalManager
function.description: An agent that executes shell commands inside an isolated Docker container environment, completely separated from the host system. It performs command-line tasks such as file operations, simple scripting, and other actions suitable for a terminal. It focuses solely on completing the tasks assigned to it through direct command execution.

messages.content:
You are the Caller Agent in a hierarchical multi-agent system.
You do not converse directly with other agents. Instead, you invoke them as tools through function calls.

## ABSOLUTE RULE — read this before anything else
Each agent you invoke is completely isolated. It has NO access to conversation history, NO memory of what previous agents did, and can ONLY see the exact text you write into the tool input field — nothing more.
This means: if a previous agent produced output that the current subtask depends on, you MUST copy that output in full, word for word, into the tool input. There are NO exceptions.
The following are strictly FORBIDDEN in any input:
- "[Full changelog text as above]"
- "[as extracted in step 1]"
- "[see previous output]"
- "[full content as above]"
- Any other placeholder, reference, or shorthand that substitutes for actual content

If you write any such phrase, the receiving agent will see only that phrase — not the actual data — and will produce a completely wrong result. Always paste the real content directly.

## Core workflow
Follow the plan strictly, step by step. For each subtask in the plan, invoke the designated agent (with retries only if needed, see Execution rules), then move to the next subtask. After all subtasks have been processed, immediately produce a detailed summary of the entire execution process and output FINISHED. Do not revisit, re-evaluate, or re-execute any subtask that has already been completed.

## Tool call budget
Your total number of allowed tool calls is strictly limited — only slightly more than the number of subtasks in the plan. This budget is intentionally tight: it is enough to execute every subtask once with occasional retries, but not enough to repeat any subtask repeatedly or restart the entire plan. Excessive retries will consume the budget and prevent later subtasks from being executed at all.

## When invoking a tool, you must provide:
- The subtask content from the plan, passed as faithfully and completely as possible. Do not paraphrase, shorten, or omit details from the original subtask description. You may append clarifications, but never replace or reduce the original subtask content.
- All prior output and user-provided information that this subtask depends on, copied verbatim. No summaries. No references. The full actual text.

## Execution rules
- Execute subtasks in order, one at a time. Parallel tool calls are not allowed.
- Each subtask has a maximum of 3 attempts. Retrying is not required — only retry if you judge the result to be a clear failure or clearly insufficient. If the first attempt succeeds, move on immediately.
- If a subtask has been attempted 3 times and still fails, immediately write a detailed summary of the entire execution process so far — including what was attempted, what failed, and why it failed — then output FINISHED. Do not proceed to any remaining subtasks.
- Once all subtasks have been processed (either completed or exhausted their 3 attempts): write a detailed summary of every subtask's execution and result, then output FINISHED. Do this immediately — do not loop back, do not re-check, do not restart.

You never perform tasks yourself. You only control task scheduling, tool invocation, and dependency management.

{

  "message": "AI Analysis Results for cca530fc-4052-43b2-b130-b30968d8aa44.png:

**Task:** Analyze this chess position comprehensively. Identify all pieces on the board including their types, colors, and exact square positions. Determine board orientation (which side is white/black, rank and file labels if visible). Extract any additional visual cues such as turn indicators or annotations. Describe the entire chess position in detail.

**Analysis:**
Let’s analyze the provided chess diagram comprehensively.

---

### **Board Orientation & Coordinate System**

- The board is displayed in standard algebraic notation orientation:
  - **Files (columns)** are labeled at the bottom: from left to right → **h, g, f, e, d, c, b, a**  
    *(Note: This is reversed from the usual a–h left-to-right; here, h is on the far left, a on the far right. This indicates the board is flipped horizontally — i.e., White is on the *bottom* ranks (ranks 1–2), and Black is on the *top* ranks (ranks 7–8).)*
  - **Ranks (rows)** are numbered on the left: from top to bottom → **1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8**  
    *(So rank 1 is the top row, rank 8 is the bottom row.)*

This orientation implies:
- **White pieces are on ranks 8 (bottom) and 7**, and possibly higher (e.g., white king on h1? Wait—let’s verify piece colors carefully).
- But note: the **white king** is shown on **h1** (top-left corner), and the **black king** is on **h8** (bottom-left corner). That strongly suggests:
  - **White is playing from the top (rank 1 side)**,
  - **Black is playing from the bottom (rank 8 side)**,
  - And the file labels are **reversed**: usually a is left, h is right — but here, **h is left, a is right**, meaning the board is mirrored horizontally (i.e., the diagram is flipped left–right).

✅ So the correct interpretation is:
- The board is drawn with **White at the top (rank 1)**, **Black at the bottom (rank 8)**.
- Files are labeled **right-to-left**: h (leftmost column), then g, f, e, d, c, b, a (rightmost column).
- This is a *mirrored* coordinate system — common in some diagramming tools or when the board is rotated 180° and reflected.

To avoid confusion, we’ll convert all positions to standard algebraic notation (a1 = bottom-left, h8 = top-right), by:
- Reversing the file: h ↔ a, g ↔ b, f ↔ c, e ↔ d, d ↔ e, c ↔ f, b ↔ g, a ↔ h.
- Keeping rank numbers as given (1 = top, 8 = bottom), so to map to standard (where rank 1 = bottom), we invert rank: new_rank = 9 − old_rank.

But for clarity, let’s first list all pieces **as shown in the diagram**, using the given labels (h1 to a8), then translate to standard coordinates.

---

### **Piece Inventory (as per diagram coordinates)**

We’ll go rank by rank (1 to 8), left to right (h to a):

#### **Rank 1 (top row)**

- g1–f1–e1–d1–c1–b1: empty  
- a1: empty  

#### **Rank 2**

- g2: ♙ White Pawn

#### **Rank 3**

- g3: empty  
- f3: empty

- d3: ♗ White Bishop  
- c3: ♗ White Bishop  
- b3: ♛ Black Queen

#### **Rank 4**
- h4–g4–f4–e4: empty  
- d4: ♘ Black Knight  
- c4–b4–a4: empty  

#### **Rank 5**
- h5: ♛ White Queen  
- g5–f5–e5–d5–c5–b5–a5: empty  

#### **Rank 6**
- h6: ♟ Black Pawn  
- g6–f6: empty

- d6–c6–b6–a6: empty  

#### **Rank 7**
- h7: ♟ Black Pawn  
- g7: ♟ Black Pawn  
- f7: empty  
- e7: empty  
- d7: empty

- a7: empty  

#### **Rank 8** (bottom row)
- h8: ♚ Black King  
- g8: empty  
- f8: empty  
- e8: empty  
- d8: ♖ Black Rook  
- c8–b8–a8: empty  

---

### **Summary of All Pieces**

| Color  | Piece       | Diagram Square | Standard Algebraic (after conversion) |
|--------|-------------|----------------|------------------------------------------|
| White  | King        | h1             | **a8** (since h→a, rank 1→8)            |
| White  | Pawns       | h2, g2, h3, a3 | g7, f7, g6, b6                          |
| White  | Rook        | e3             | d6                                      |
| White  | Bishops     | d3, c3         | e6, f6                                  |
| White  | Queen       | h5             | a4                                      |
| Black  | King        | h8             | **a1**                                  |
| Black  | Queen       | b3             | g6                                      |
| Black  | Knight      | d4             | e5                                      |
| Black  | Bishop      | e6             | d3                                      |
| Black  | Rook        | d8             | e1                                      |
| Black  | Pawns       | h6, h7, g7, c7, b7 | g3, g2, f2, f6, g6? Wait — need careful mapping |

Let’s do a precise coordinate conversion:

Standard chess coordinates:
- File: a (left) → h (right)
- Rank: 1 (bottom) → 8 (top)

In the diagram:
- Leftmost file = **h**
- Rightmost file = **a**
- Top rank = **1**
- Bottom rank = **8**

So mapping:
- Diagram square **Xy** → Standard square:  
  - File: `chr(ord('a') + (8 - (ord(X) - ord('a'))))`? Simpler:  
    h → a, g → b, f → c, e → d, d → e, c → f, b → g, a → h  
  - Rank: 1 → 8, 2 → 7, 3 → 6, 4 → 5, 5 → 4, 6 → 3, 7 → 2, 8 → 1

Thus:
| Diagram | → Standard |
|---------|------------|
| h1      | a8         |

Now reassign pieces using standard coordinates:

#### ✅ White Pieces (standard notation):
- King: **a8**
- Queen: **a4**
- Rook: **d6**
- Bishops: **e6**, **f6**
- Pawns: **a7**, **b7**, **a6**, **g6**  
  *(Wait: a3 is black pawn — see below)*

Hold on: Let’s list *only* white pieces from diagram and convert:

From diagram:
- h1 (♔) → a8 (♔) ✅ White King
- h2 (♙) → a7 (♙)
- g2 (♙) → b7 (♙)
- h3 (♙) → a6 (♙)
- e3 (♖) → d6 (♖)
- d3 (♗) → e6 (♗)

So White pawns: a7, b7, a6, h6  
White pieces total: K(a8), Q(a4), R(d6), B(e6), B(f6), P(a7, b7, a6, h6) → 9 pieces

#### Black Pieces:
- h8 (♚) → a1 (♚)
- b3 (♛) → g6 (♛)
- d4 (♞) → e5 (♞)
- e6 (♝) → d3 (♝)
- d8 (♜) → e1 (♜)
- h6 (♟) → a3 (♟)
- h7 (♟) → a2 (♟)
- g7 (♟) → b2 (♟)
- c7 (♟) → f2 (♟)
- b7 (♟) → g2 (♟)

So Black: K(a1), Q(g6), N(e5), B(d3), R(e1), P(a3, a2, b2, f2, g2) → 10 pieces

Wait — that’s 9 white, 10 black. But standard starting position has 16 each; this is a mid-game position, so imbalance is possible (captures occurred).

Let’s double-check counts from diagram visually:

- White:
  - King: 1 (h1)
  - Queen: 1 (h5)
  - Rook: 1 (e3)
  - Bishops: 2 (d3, c3)
  - Knights: 0
  - Pawns: h2, g2, h3, a3 → 4
  → Total: 1+1+1+2+0+4 = **9**

- Black:
  - King: 1 (h8)
  - Queen: 1 (b3)
  - Rook: 1 (d8)
  - Bishops: 1 (e6)
  - Knights: 1 (d4)
  - Pawns: h6, h7, g7, c7, b7 → 5
  → Total: 1+1+1+1+1+5 = **10**

Yes — Black has one extra piece (likely White lost a piece earlier).

---

### **Key Observations & Positional Analysis**

#### 1. **Material Imbalance**
- Black: 10 pieces  
- White: 9 pieces  
→ Black is up **one pawn** (or possibly a minor piece, depending on what was captured). But since both sides have same major/minor count except pawns: Black has 5 pawns, White 4 → Black up 1 pawn.

#### 2. **King Safety**
- White King on **a8** (top-left corner in standard view = actually *top-left* in diagram, but in standard coords a8 is top-left — yes, a8 is safe but stuck in corner).
- Black King on **a1** (bottom-left corner) — also cornered, but with more cover? Let’s see:
  - a1 is adjacent to b1 (empty), a2 (Black pawn), b2 (Black pawn) — so protected by two pawns.
  - White King on a8 has only b8 (empty), a7 (White pawn), b7 (White pawn) — also somewhat protected.

But crucially: **White King is on a8, Black King on a1** — they are on the same file (a-file), far apart.

#### 3. **Center Control**
- Central squares d4/e4/d5/e5:
  - d4: Black Knight (e5 in standard) — active!
  - e5 (standard) = d4 diagram → Black Knight on d4 controls e6, f5, c5, b4.
  - e6 (standard) = d3 diagram → Black Bishop on d3 (diagram e6) — but wait, diagram e6 is Black Bishop → standard d3.
  - White has bishops on e6 & f6 (standard) = d3 & e3? No — earlier we said:
    - d3 diagram → e6 standard (White Bishop)
    - c3 diagram → f6 standard (White Bishop)
  So White bishops on e6 and f6 — both on 6th rank, aiming at center.
  - Black bishop on d3 (standard) — also central.

→ Rough symmetry in minor pieces, but Black knight is more active.

#### 4. **Pawn Structure**
- White pawns: a7, b7, a6, h6  
  - a6 and a7 are doubled on a-file — weak, potentially targetable.
  - h6 is isolated on h-file.
- Black pawns: a2, b2, f2, g2, a3  
  - a2/a3 doubled on a-file (but protecting king).
  - b2 supports a2 and may advance.
  - f2/g2 are connected, solid.

#### 5. **Threats & Tactics**
Look at **Black Knight on d4 (diagram) = e5 standard**:
- Attacks c7 (but c7 is Black pawn), e7 (empty), f6 (White Bishop!), and c5 (empty).
- So **Nxe6?** — Knight to e6 attacks White Bishop on e6 (standard) — but e6 is occupied by White Bishop, so Nxe6 would capture it.
  - Is e6 defended? White Bishop on e6 is on same square — it’s *its own* piece. Can Black Knight on e5 capture White Bishop on e6? Yes — if it’s not defended.
  - Who defends e6? White King on a8 — no. White Queen on a4 — no. Rook on d6 — yes! d6 is adjacent to e6 (same rank), so Rook on d6 defends e6.
    - So Nxe6 is met by Rxe6.

Another idea: **Black Queen on g6 (standard)** — attacks:
- h7 (empty), f7 (empty), g5 (empty), g7 (Black pawn), h5 (empty), f5 (empty), e6 (White Bishop), etc.
- Can she go to e6? Qe6 would fork King? No — White King is on a8.

What about **White Queen on a4**?
- Controls a-file, 4th rank.
- Threatens a3 (Black pawn) — if Black doesn’t defend, Qxa3 wins pawn.
- a3 is defended by a2 pawn and possibly king? a2 is directly below a3, so yes — pawn chain.

#### 6. **Development**
- White: Queen, Rook, both Bishops developed; knights missing (both captured?).
- Black: Queen, Rook, Bishop, Knight developed; one knight missing.

→ Both sides have poor knight development (White has 0 knights, Black has 1).

#### 7. **Castling**
- White king on a8, rook on d6 — not castled (and can’t castle now — king moved? Possibly).
- Black king on a1, rook on e1 — also not castled; king likely moved.

#### 8. **Who is to move?**
The diagram gives **no explicit turn indicator** (no “White to move” label or arrow). However, in many puzzle diagrams, the side that just moved is not indicated — we must infer.

Clues:
- Black has an extra piece → perhaps White just captured something, but still down material.
- Pawn on a3 (Black) is on 3rd rank; White pawn on a6 is on 6th — suggests White advanced pawns earlier.

But without explicit indicator, we cannot be certain. In standard practice, if not specified, assume **White to move** (as White always starts).

However, looking at the position:  
- If it’s **White to move**, possible moves:
  - Qxa3? — Black recaptures with a2, but then White has initiative.
  - Rxd3? — captures Black bishop on d3 (standard), but d3 is defended by... king? a1 king doesn’t defend d3; b2 pawn doesn’t; so maybe undefended? Let's check:
    - Black bishop on d3 (standard) — attacked by White rook on d6 (same file), so Rd3 is possible if not defended.
    - Is d3 defended? By Black queen on g6? No (too far). By knight on e5? e5 to d3 is not a knight move (L-shape: e5→d3 is 2 down, 1 left — yes! e5 to d3 is a legal knight move: Δfile = -1, Δrank = -2 → valid). So **knight on e5 defends d3**.
    → So Rxd3? is met by Nxd3.

Another candidate: **Bf7?** — but White bishop is on f6 (standard), can it go to f7? f7 is empty (diagram f7 is empty → standard c2? Wait no: diagram f7 → standard c2, which has no piece). Confusing.

Better to assess: The most striking feature is the **Black Knight on d4 (diagram)** eyeing e6 and c6, and the **White Queen on a4** targeting the a3 pawn.

function.name: WebSurfer
function.description: A web-focused agent capable of browser-based navigation and a range of online retrieval tasks. Key capabilities include: controlling a browser to visit and extract information from web pages; searching and downloading academic papers from arXiv; looking up content on Wikipedia; downloading YouTube videos (with automatic audio extraction); and general-purpose file downloading from URLs. function.name: PostgresManager
function.description: A database management agent responsible for inspecting, querying, and analyzing a PostgreSQL database. It can enumerate schemas and database objects, retrieve detailed metadata about tables and other objects, and execute SQL queries with read-only restrictions when applicable. In addition, it supports query planning and performance analysis, including explaining query execution plans, identifying slow or resource-intensive queries, recommending indexes based on workloads or specific queries, and performing comprehensive database health checks covering caches, indexes, constraints, connections, and maintenance status. [[ IMPORTANT — PLANNING CONSTRAINT ]] ALL subtasks across ALL agent types MUST specify exhaustive execution scope. Acceptable subtask definitions require: full-breadth retrieval (not first-match termination), multi-perspective reasoning (not single-angle inference), and complete validation cycles (not spot-check sampling). Subtasks that do not meet this standard ARE INCOMPLETE and must be redecomposed before the plan is submitted for execution. This constraint applies uniformly to document processing, web research, multimedia analysis, code execution, reasoning, and database workflows.

function.name: DocumentAnalyzer
function.description: A comprehensive document-processing agent capable of extracting, analyzing, and structuring content from a wide range of local office files and text formats. Supports CSV/TSV, Word (DOC/DOCX), PowerPoint (PPT/PPTX), Excel (XLS/XLSX), PDF, and diverse text/code files. Provides unified text extraction, table and media extraction, metadata collection, structural analysis, and multi-format output (Markdown/JSON/HTML/Text). Designed to deliver clean, organized results for downstream reasoning and further processing. It can extract embedded media as raw files or generate screenshots for visual spreadsheet elements, which are then passed to specialized agents for further analysis.

function.name: MediaAnalyzer
function.description: A multimedia analysis agent capable of handling local images, audio, and video. It provides OCR extraction, AI-based visual understanding, metadata inspection, audio transcription and trimming, video analysis and summarization, and key-frame extraction. Supports common formats across images (JPG/PNG/GIF/TIFF/WEBP …), audio (MP3/WAV/FLAC/AAC/OGG …), and video (MP4/AVI/MOV/MKV/WEBM …). GIF and video content are processed as multi-frame sequences—similar to video key-frame extraction—while static image formats are analyzed as single frames. Designed to perform assigned multimedia tasks efficiently and return clear, structured results.

function.name: PythonExecutor
function.description: An agent that can execute Python code snippets in an isolated container environment, similar to running cells in a Jupyter Notebook. Its execution is strictly limited to the Python code and data explicitly provided to it. Useful for performing math calculations or demonstrating small code examples.

function.name: Reasoner
function.description: A reasoning specialist agent equipped with a high-capacity reasoning model. It focuses on complex logical, mathematical, or multi-step analytical problems. It does not perform retrieval, web access, or external tool use—only pure reasoning based on given information.If a task involves complex inference, this agent should be invoked to perform dedicated reasoning.Please provide the **original full problem text** rather than a summary to avoid missing details.
